era: Bengal village school days to the scattered present
target_audience: readers who remember their school friends, the village and its small things, and the feelings that time could not take
book_summary: A cycle of forty poems spoken by one who calls 'Friend, where are you?' into the years that scattered forty schoolmates — twenty boys and twenty girls — from a Bengal village. Each poem opens one human emotion and lets it surface through a single small thing of childhood: a shared tiffin, a monsoon walk, a song under the banyan, a hand held at the edge of the field. The poems move through courage, longing, joy, envy, forgiveness, faith, grief, tenderness, and at last the peace of reconnection, until the roll-call of forty names becomes the talk of the mind and the touch of the hand made whole again.
gist: Forty school friends — twenty boys and twenty girls — reach back across the years to reconnect, because a life is not a life without the talk of the mind, the shared feeling, and the simple touch; together they summon every human emotion and let it surface through the nostalgia of a Bengal village and the small, freely-offered things of childhood.

chapters.chapter_summary: The school bell and the calling of names on the first morning, when forty children answered one by one. The poem opens on the sound of a name spoken aloud, and asks what is lost when a voice no longer answers.
The midday box opened between two friends, the rice and the small fish shared without counting. The poem renders generosity as the simplest arithmetic, the thing given freely that is never measured.
The way home turned to mud under the first rain, and two children walked it holding hands so neither would slip. The poem follows the path as a bond that only a hard season could make firm.
A song taught beneath the great tree, its tune returning years later uninvited. The poem lets the melody be a doorway through which the whole village walks back in.
Two children at one slate, the chalk passed between them while the teacher's back was turned. The poem remembers the first shared secret of the classroom.
The boy who could never come first, and the sourness he carried like a stone in his pocket. The poem looks at envy not as sin but as a wound the village never taught him to name.
A quarrel and its quiet end, the hand offered again after words too sharp to take back. The poem holds the moment when anger loosens into something like grace.
The girl who carried water at dawn, her first kindness a cup offered without being asked. The poem remembers thirst as the beginning of tenderness.
The kite torn free and carried over the paddy, two friends watching it go without regret. The poem lets the lost thing stand for every ambition that outgrew the village.
The evening study by one lamp, the wick trimmed low, the same page read by two pairs of eyes. The poem renders shared light as the first intimacy of the mind.

chapters.chapter_title: The Courage of the First Answer
chapters.chapter_summary: The child who stood to answer when no one else would, voice shaking. The poem names courage not as boldness but as the small rising of a frightened voice.
A promise made at the pond's edge, to always be friends, the water keeping it better than any tongue. The poem weighs a child's vow against the years that followed.
A book lent and never returned, its pages now in a stranger's house. The poem lets a small debt carry the weight of every kindness that went uncounted.
The brush of a hand passing something across the bench, remembered years later with sudden clarity. The poem holds the body's memory against the mind's forgetting.
The friend who left the village first, and the ache that followed him to the city. The poem follows longing as a road that runs in one direction only.
The football kicked into the goal at dusk, the whole field shouting one name. The poem remembers joy as a thing shared so fully it became the air itself.
The bitter neem under which secrets were told, its shade keeping them. The poem lets the tree witness what the friends could not say elsewhere.

chapters.chapter_title: The Grief of the One Who Left
chapters.chapter_summary: The friend who died young, whose bench stayed empty the rest of the year. The poem sits with grief as the one feeling that never found its way into a single word.
The rival grown older, his stone of envy worn smooth to a pebble. The poem returns to rivalry and finds only the long shadow of a shared childhood.
A word given and kept, a promise that held when nothing else did. The poem names faith as the rarest of the small things, given freely and never taken back.
The first rain caught in the courtyard, hands cupped to hold it. The poem renders wonder as the village's own religion, before any other was taught.
The joke that broke the whole bench into laughter, food forgotten. The poem remembers laughter as the only sound that needs no translation across the years.

chapters.chapter_title: The Shyness of the First Word
chapters.chapter_summary: The word too shy to be spoken, left on the slate instead. The poem traces shyness as the seed of every feeling that later learned to speak.
The river where the friends bathed and talked of the future, the current carrying their words downstream. The poem lets the river be the one listener that never judged.
The thing never said, the thanks never given, now spoken only to memory. The poem holds regret as a door that opens too late.
The letter sent to a far city and the waiting for an answer. The poem follows hope as a small flame kept alive against the distance.

chapters.chapter_title: The Tenderness of the Mother's Hand
chapters.chapter_summary: The mother who packed the tiffin, her hand brushing the child's head. The poem remembers tenderness as the first feeling, before any friend had a name.

chapters.chapter_title: The Pride of the Small Win
chapters.chapter_summary: The small victory in a school game, the chest puffed for an afternoon. The poem weighs pride as the first taste of being seen.
The child who always asked why, and the teacher who never tired. The poem honors curiosity as the hunger that kept the village's mind awake.

chapters.chapter_title: The Gratitude for the Small Loan
chapters.chapter_summary: The coin lent for the fair and returned the next day. The poem names gratitude as the weight of a debt that joy alone could repay.

chapters.chapter_title: The Wonder of the First Train
chapters.chapter_summary: The first glimpse of a train, its smoke over the fields. The poem lets the machine stand for every departure the friends could not yet imagine.
The bench emptied one by one as the friends left, until a single child sat alone. The poem sits with loneliness as the quiet after the roll-call.

chapters.chapter_title: The Compassion of the Shared Umbrella
chapters.chapter_summary: One umbrella over three heads in the rain, the one who held it going wet. The poem renders compassion as the choice to be soaked so another stays dry.
The smell of rice cooking at dusk, remembered in a far kitchen. The poem lets a single scent carry the whole village across the years.
The secret told and kept, the two who shared it bound forever. The poem names trust as the thread that the scattered years could not cut.
Sitting at the field's edge at harvest, needing nothing more. The poem finds contentment in the plain abundance of the village, before ambition arrived.
A debt of hurt forgiven without a word, the quarrel simply outgrown. The poem returns to forgiveness as the one feeling that ends by freeing both.
The phone call that began 'Friend, where are you?', and the voice that answered. The poem holds the sound of a name spoken after many years.
The meeting again, the handclasp that said everything the years had not. The poem lets a single touch finish the sentence that distance had begun.

The roll-call spoken once more at dusk, all forty names answered at last. The poem closes the cycle where the call 'Friend, where are you?' becomes its own answer, and the village keeps the small things waiting.
